newsitem.title: THAILAND: Finance woes, tax hike double blow to Thai firms.
newsitem.headline: Finance woes, tax hike double blow to Thai firms.

text.p: Turbulence in the financial sector and a planned tax rise should dampen corporate activity in Thailand although an export-led recovery is likely in the longer term, analysts said on Thursday.

Thai manufacturers and retailers were likely to see a sharp drop in sales, especially in luxury goods such as cars, as consumers reduced spending after value-added tax (VAT) rose from seven percent to 10 percent on August 16, they said.
An analyst at an American brokerage said the planned tax hike would hurt Thai consumption, dragging down already slow economic growth.
Thai interest rates, meanwhile, are expected to stay high due to a lingering liquidity crisis that has led to the abrupt suspension of two thirds of Thai finance firms.

The Thai financial sector has been in paralysis under the weight of "bubble era" bad loans to the property sector. The liquidity crunch has made it costly for companies to raise funds for fresh capital investment.
"It's inevitable that the financial move would have an effect on business, and VAT hike does not help," said Ian Mclennan, head of research at SBC Warburg.

He said that Thai business would face a tough time in the next three to six months, partly because two to three months would be needed to overcome the fallout from the suspension of finance companies.
Several Japanese vehicle manufacturers said on Thursday they planned to cut production at their Thai plants to reduce inventories.

Truck maker Isuzu Motors Ltd said its Thai output of large to medium-sized trucks would fall by more than 30 percent in the year to March 1998 because the de facto devaluation of the baht and a rise in local interest rates were affecting its business.
Mitsubishi Motors Corp said it would produce a total of 50,000 cars and pick-up trucks at its Thai plants in 1997 for the local market against output of 73,000 in 1996.

"It will take some time before the effect from the flotation of the baht becomes clear. We think, however, that it will probably further dampen demand but will be good for exports," a Mitsubishi Motor spokesman said in Tokyo.
The VAT hike was among economic measures announced by the Thai government on Tuesday in an effort to pull the economy from its worst slump in more than a decade.
The package included pledges to maintain $25 billion in foreign reserves, balance the budget, trim inflation, cut the current account deficit and continue tight monetary policy.
In exchange for the austerity measures, Bangkok is seeking financial help of up to $12-$15 billion from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other nations.
The economic package came about a month after Bangkok made a surprise decision to float the baht, triggering a plunge in the currency's value by about 20 percent.
Analysts said they felt the Thai economy would pick up in the long term, drawing strength from a possible recovery in exports. A weak baht favours Thai exports by making them more competitive abroad.
"The falling value of the baht will help industrial output in about six months, and I think an export-led economic recovery would eventually come," said SBC Warburg's Mclennan.
